content.narrative_summary: This page continues the Methods section, describing the ESC guideline development process, including iterative Task Force votes, declaration-of-interest reviews, and coordination by the ESC CPG Committee. It notes funding sources, review rounds, and considerations for off-label medication use. It then begins the Introduction, summarizing new evidence since the 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines in a bulleted list covering: shared decision-making by Heart Teams; advanced imaging modalities; accurate assessment of valve disease mechanisms; expanded evidence for aortic stenosis interventions; refined decision-making criteria for TAVI/SAVR; mid-term TAVI safety in low-risk patients; TAVI indications in bicuspid AV and AR; mitral regurgitation intervention advances; longer-term data on secondary MR; evolving tricuspid valve treatment evidence; improved guidance for mixed VHD; updated SVD definitions; revised DOAC recommendations; and new sex-specific VHD considerations.

content.narrative_summary: This section introduces updates in the 2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease, noting scope exclusions (e.g., infective endocarditis, chronic coronary syndrome, atrial fibrillation, aortic or congenital disease) and emphasizing concise, practical recommendations. It highlights factors influencing individual treatment decisions, the role of equipment and expertise, and the importance of a collaborative multidisciplinary Heart Team approach.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 3 New recommendations

rows.recommendation: Omission of invasive coronary angiography should be considered in TAVI candidates, if procedural planning CT angiography is of sufficient quality to rule out significant CAD.
PCI should be considered in patients with a primary indication to undergo TAVI and ≥90% coronary artery stenosis in segments with a reference diameter ≥2.5 mm.
TAVI may be considered for the treatment of severe AR in symptomatic patients ineligible for surgery according to the Heart Team, if the anatomy is suitable.

Intervention should be considered in asymptomatic patients (confirmed by a normal exercise test, if feasible) with severe, high-gradient AS and LVEF ≥50%, as an alternative to close active surveillance, if the procedural risk is low.
TAVI may be considered for the treatment of severe BAV stenosis in patients at increased surgical risk, if the anatomy is suitable.

Surgical MV repair is recommended in low-risk asymptomatic patients with severe PMR without LV dysfunction (LVESD <40 mm, LVESDi <20 mm/m², and LVEF >60%) when a durable result is likely, if at least three of the following criteria are fulfilled: AF; SPAP at rest ≥50 mmHg; LA dilatation (LAVI ≥60 mL/m² or LA diameter ≥55 mm); Concomitant secondary TR ≥ moderate.
Minimally invasive MV surgery may be considered at experienced centres to reduce the length of stay and accelerate recovery.
MV surgery, surgical AF ablation, if indicated, and LAAO should be considered in symptomatic patients with severe atrial SMR under optimal medical therapy.
TEER may be considered in symptomatic patients with severe atrial SMR not eligible for surgery after optimization of medical therapy including rhythm control, when appropriate.
MV surgery may be considered in patients with moderate SMR undergoing CABG.
TMVI may be considered in symptomatic patients with extensive MAC and severe MV dysfunction at experienced Heart Valve Centres with expertise in complex MV surgery and transcatheter interventions.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents Table 4 “Revised recommendations,” comparing recommendations from the 2021 and 2025 guideline versions across four clinical contexts: coronary artery disease in valvular heart disease, atrial fibrillation in native valvular heart disease, indications for surgery in severe aortic regurgitation, and intervention in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis. recommendation_tables.title: Table 4 Revised recommendations

rows.recommendation: CCTA should be considered as an alternative to coronary angiography before valve surgery in patients with severe VHD and low probability of CAD.
CCTA is recommended before valve intervention in patients with moderate or lower (≤50%) pre-test likelihood of obstructive CAD.

Coronary angiography is recommended before valve surgery in patients with severe VHD and any of the following:
• History of cardiovascular disease
• Suspected myocardial ischaemia
• LV systolic dysfunction
• In men >40 years of age and post-menopausal women
• One or more cardiovascular risk factors.
Invasive coronary angiography is recommended before valve intervention in patients with high and very high (>50%) pre-test likelihood of obstructive CAD.
Coronary angiography is recommended in the evaluation of severe SMR.
Invasive coronary angiography is recommended in the evaluation of CAD in patients with severe ventricular SMR.
PCI should be considered in patients with a primary indication to undergo TAVI and coronary artery diameter stenosis ≥70% in proximal segments.
PCI may be considered in patients with a primary indication to undergo transcatheter valve interventions and coronary artery stenosis ≥70% in proximal segments of main vessels.
PCI should be considered in patients with a primary indication to undergo transcatheter MV intervention and coronary artery diameter stenosis >70% in proximal segments.
LAAO should be considered to reduce the thromboembolic risk in patients with AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 undergoing valve surgery.
Surgical closure of the LA appendage is recommended as an adjunct to OAC in patients with AF undergoing valve surgery to prevent cardioembolic stroke and systemic thromboembolism.

Concomitant AF ablation should be considered in patients undergoing valve surgery, balancing the benefits of freedom from atrial arrhythmias and the risk factors for recurrence (LA dilatation, years in AF, age, renal dysfunction, and other cardiovascular risk factors).

Concomitant surgical ablation is recommended in patients undergoing MV surgery with AF suitable for a rhythm control strategy to prevent symptoms and recurrence of AF, according to an experienced team of electrophysiologists and arrhythmia surgeons.

Concomitant surgical ablation should be considered in patients undergoing non-MV surgery with AF suitable for a rhythm control strategy to prevent symptoms and recurrence of AF, according to an experienced team of electrophysiologists and arrhythmia surgeons.
The use of DOACs is not recommended in patients with AF and moderate-to-severe MS.
The use of DOACs is not recommended in patients with AF and rheumatic MS with an MVA ≤2.0 cm².
AV repair may be considered in selected patients at experienced centres when durable results are expected.
AV repair should be considered in selected patients with severe AR at experienced centres, when durable results are expected.
Surgery may be considered in asymptomatic patients with LVESD >20 mm/m² BSA (especially in patients with small body size) or resting LVEF ≤55%, if surgery is at low risk.

AV surgery may be considered in asymptomatic patients with severe AR and LVESDi >22 mm/m² or LVESVi >45 mL/m² [especially in patients with small body size (BSA <1.68 m²)], or resting LVEF ≤55%, if surgical risk is low.
Intervention is recommended in symptomatic patients with severe low-flow (SVI ≤35 mL/m²), low-gradient (<40 mmHg) AS with reduced LVEF (<50%), and evidence of flow (contractile) reserve.
Intervention is recommended in symptomatic patients with low-flow (SVI ≤35 mL/m²), low-gradient (<40 mmHg) AS with reduced LVEF (<50%) after careful confirmation that AS is severe.

recommendation_tables.title: Indications for intervention in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis—Section 8.5

rows.recommendation: Intervention should be considered in asymptomatic patients with severe AS and LV dysfunction (LVEF <55%) without another cause.

Intervention should be considered in asymptomatic patients with LVEF >55% and a normal exercise test if the procedural risk is low and one of the following parameters is present:
• Very severe AS (mean gradient ≥60 mmHg or Vmax >5 m/s).
• Severe valve calcification (ideally assessed by CCT) and Vmax progression ≥0.3 m/s/year.
• Markedly elevated BNP levels (more than three times age- and sex-corrected normal range) confirmed by repeated measurements and without other explanation.

Intervention should be considered in asymptomatic patients with severe AS and LVEF ≥50%, if the procedural risk is low and one of the following parameters is present:
• Very severe AS (mean gradient ≥60 mmHg or Vmax >5.0 m/s).
• Severe valve calcification (ideally assessed by CCT) and Vmax progression >0.3 m/s/year.
• Markedly elevated BNP/NT-proBNP levels (more than three times age- and sex-corrected normal range, confirmed on repeated measurement without other explanation).
• LVEF <55% without another cause.

recommendation_tables.title: Mode of intervention in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis—Section 8.5

rows.recommendation: The choice between surgical and transcatheter intervention must be based upon careful evaluation of clinical, anatomical, and procedural factors by the Heart Team, weighing the risks and benefits of each approach for an individual patient. The Heart Team recommendation should be discussed with the patient who can then make an informed treatment choice.

It is recommended that the mode of intervention is based on Heart Team assessment of individual clinical, anatomical, and procedural characteristics, incorporating lifetime management considerations and estimated life expectancy.
TAVI is recommended in older patients (≥75 years), or in those who are high risk (STS-PROM/EuroSCORE II >8%) or unsuitable for surgery.
TAVI is recommended in patients ≥70 years of age with tricuspid AV stenosis, if the anatomy is suitable.
SAVR is recommended in younger patients who are low risk for surgery (<75 years and STS-PROM/EuroSCORE II <4%), or in patients who are operable and unsuitable for transfemoral TAVI.
SAVR is recommended in patients <70 years of age, if the surgical risk is low.
SAVR or TAVI are recommended for all remaining candidates for an aortic BHV according to Heart Team assessment.1–4
Non-transfemoral TAVI may be considered in patients who are inoperable and unsuitable for transfemoral TAVI.
Non-transfemoral TAVI should be considered in patients who are unsuitable for surgery and transfemoral access.

recommendation_tables.title: Indications for intervention in severe primary mitral regurgitation—Section 9.1.4

rows.recommendation: Surgery should be considered in asymptomatic patients with preserved LV function (LVESD <40 mm and LVEF >60%) and AF secondary to MR or PH (SPAP at rest >50 mmHg).

MV surgery should be considered in asymptomatic patients with severe PMR without LV dysfunction (LVESD <40 mm, LVESDi <20 mm/m^2, and LVEF >60%) in the presence of PH (SPAP at rest >50 mmHg), or AF secondary to MR.

Surgical MV repair should be considered in low-risk asymptomatic patients with LVEF >60%, LVESD <40 mm, and significant LA dilatation (volume index ≥60 mL/m^2 or diameter ≥55 mm) when performed in a Heart Valve Centre and a durable repair is likely.

Surgical MV repair should be considered in low-risk asymptomatic patients with severe PMR without LV dysfunction (LVESD <40 mm, LVESDi <20 mm/m^2, and LVEF >60%) in the presence of significant LA dilatation (LAVI ≥60 mL/m^2 or LA diameter ≥55 mm), when performed in a Heart Valve Centre and a durable repair is likely.

rows.recommendation: TEER should be considered in selected symptomatic patients not eligible for surgery and fulfilling criteria suggesting an increased chance of responding to the treatment.

In high-risk symptomatic patients not eligible for surgery and not fulfilling the criteria suggesting an increased chance of responding to TEER, the Heart Team may consider in selected cases a TEER procedure or other transcatheter valve therapy if applicable, after careful evaluation of ventricular assist device or heart transplant.

rows.recommendation: Surgery is recommended in patients with severe primary TR undergoing left-sided valve surgery.

Transcatheter, transfemoral valve-in-valve implantation in the aortic position should be considered by the Heart Team depending on anatomical considerations, features of the prosthesis, and in patients who are at high operative risk or inoperable.

Transcatheter transfemoral valve-in-valve implantation in the aortic position should be considered in patients with significant valve dysfunction who are at intermediate or high surgical risk, and have suitable anatomical and prosthesis features, as assessed by the Heart Team.
Transcatheter valve-in-valve implantation in the mitral and tricuspid position may be considered in selected patients at high risk for surgical reintervention.

recommendation_tables.title: Management of mechanical heart valve thrombosis—Section 14.4

rows.recommendation: Urgent or emergency valve replacement is recommended for obstructive thrombosis in critically ill patients without serious comorbidity.

Heart Team evaluation is recommended in patients with acute HF (NYHA class III or IV) due to obstructive MHV thrombosis to determine appropriate management (repeat valve replacement or low-dose slow infusion fibrinolysis).

Fibrinolysis (using recombinant tissue plasminogen activator 10 mg bolus + 90 mg in 90 min with UFH or streptokinase 1 500 000 U in 60 min without UFH) should be considered when surgery is not available or is very high risk, or for thrombosis of right-sided prostheses.

rows.recommendation: Anticoagulation using a VKA and/or UFH is recommended in BHV thrombosis before considering reintervention.

content.title: 8.4 Indication for intervention
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses indications for valve intervention in aortic stenosis (AS). In symptomatic severe AS, early intervention is strongly recommended, with specific management strategies differing for low-flow, low-gradient AS with reduced or preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and normal-flow, low-gradient AS. Intervention should not be delayed by medical therapy but should precede or accompany heart failure (HF) management. In asymptomatic severe AS, up to 40% of patients are symptom‐free at diagnosis; exercise testing can uncover latent symptoms and guide treatment. Early intervention may be considered for asymptomatic patients with severe AS and LVEF <50% or adverse prognostic features. The section also reviews randomized controlled trials comparing early transcatheter or surgical aortic valve replacement (TAVR/SAVR) versus surveillance, noting reductions in cardiovascular events but variable trial power and follow‐up. It begins into moderate AS, noting that intervention in moderate AS is usually reserved for patients undergoing other cardiac surgery and that evidence linking moderate AS to outcomes in patients with reduced EF is evolving.

section_headings: 8.5.1. The mode of intervention in candidates for a bioprosthesis
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses selection of aortic valve (AV) intervention based on patient characteristics, including life expectancy, prosthesis durability, and preferences. Surgical bioprosthetic valves (BHV) via SAVR or TAVI are common in Europe and North America, with BHVs requiring no long-term anticoagulation but limited durability, while mechanical heart valves (MHV) offer durability at the cost of lifelong anticoagulation and bleeding risk. MHVs are preferred for patients younger than 60–65 years; BHVs for those older. The Ross procedure is highlighted for younger patients desiring no anticoagulation, though it has technical complexity and mid-term reintervention rates. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty and TAVI are discussed as alternatives in high-risk or inoperable patients. Registry data indicate increasing use of TAVI, yet access and variation persist globally. Meta-analyses of randomized trials comparing TAVI versus SAVR in varying surgical risk populations show similar or improved short-term outcomes with TAVI but higher rates of specific complications such as paravalvular leak and pacemaker implantation.

content.narrative_summary: In a multicentre registry of over 1300 patients with primary mitral regurgitation (PMR), elevated BNP levels independently predicted long-term mortality under medical treatment, whereas pre-operative BNP activation did not affect post-surgical mortality. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is described as an alternative gold standard for precise quantification of regurgitant volume and fraction and for determination of cardiac volumes using combined planimetered volumetric and phase-contrast methods; in Barlow’s disease with annular disjunction, CMR-detected myocardial fibrosis is linked to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. Cardiac computed tomography provides high-resolution anatomical detail of the mitral valve apparatus and is increasingly important for intervention planning, including assessment of arterial access for extracorporeal circulation, evaluation of mitral valve calcification for minimally invasive surgery, and feasibility of transcatheter mitral valve implantation based on annulus size and LVOT obstruction risk.

section_headings: 14.4 Management of prosthetic valve dysfunction and complications
content.narrative_summary: Section 14.4 defines prosthetic valve dysfunction, distinguishing structural valve deterioration (SVD) from non-structural dysfunction, and notes that valve thrombosis and endocarditis are separate but related entities. Subsection 14.4.1 describes SVD—leaflet wear, disruption, fibrosis or calcification, and stent or strut deformation—more common in bioprosthetic versus mechanical valves. It recommends serial transthoracic echocardiography at discharge and within 1–3 months post-implantation. Diagnosis of moderate or severe haemodynamic valve deterioration should prompt referral to a Heart Valve Centre for advanced imaging (TOE, CCT, PET-CT) and Heart Team discussion of redo surgery versus transcatheter valve-in-valve implantation, considering anatomical and procedural risks such as LVOT obstruction, coronary obstruction, and need for pacing.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues guidance on non-cardiac surgery (NCS) in severe aortic stenosis (AS). Urgent low- and intermediate-risk NCS can be performed safely, while deferred NCS requires pre-operative Heart Team evaluation to choose SAVR or TAVI, with TAVI preferred in elderly or complex/high-risk cases. Treatment of asymptomatic severe AS should be individualized. Section 15.2.2 advises controlling heart rate and fluid balance to prevent pulmonary oedema in mitral stenosis, avoiding arterial vasodilators, and notes that non-cardiac surgery is safe in patients with MVA >1.5 cm² or asymptomatic patients with MVA ≤1.5 cm² and SPAP <50 mm Hg. Section 15.2.3 states that non-cardiac surgery in asymptomatic patients with severe MR or AR and preserved LV function is usually safe; urgent surgery in severe ventricular SMR requires strict haemodynamic monitoring, and for elective intermediate/high-risk cases, medical optimisation and consideration of TEER after Heart Team discussion are recommended.

content.narrative_summary: Section 15.3 covers peri-operative monitoring, emphasizing heart-rate control (particularly in mitral stenosis) and careful fluid management (particularly in aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation with reduced LVEF), involvement of specialized cardiovascular anaesthesiologists, optional TOE monitoring, and noting that pulmonary artery catheterization is not routinely used. content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of sex differences in surgical and transcatheter aortic valve replacement (SAVR vs TAVI), noting higher male referral and benefit, and lower mortality but higher complications in elderly women. Indexed cut‐offs for aortic regurgitation require further study. Under 17.2, mitral valve disease from rheumatic heart disease disproportionately affects young women, with limited access to balloon valvuloplasty in low‐income settings. Fibroelastic disease causes mitral annular abnormalities, and women experience lower LV end‐systolic dimensions but similar LVEF cut‐offs with higher mortality. Secondary MR and atrial SMR patterns differ by sex, and female sex is a risk factor for mitral annular calcification with faster progression. Section 17.3 describes tricuspid regurgitation as more prevalent in women, associated with HFpEF and AF, typically diagnosed later, and with similar surgical and transcatheter outcomes. Reoperation is recommended if a PVL is related to endocarditis, or causes haemolysis requiring repeated blood transfusion or leading to HF symptoms.
Reoperation is recommended in symptomatic patients with significant valve dysfunction not attributable to valve thrombosis.
Reintervention is recommended in symptomatic patients with significant valve dysfunction not attributable to valve thrombosis.
TOE and/or 4D-CT are recommended in patients with suspected valve thrombosis to confirm the diagnosis.

rows.recommendation: Heart Team evaluation is recommended in patients with acute HF (NYHA class III or IV) due to obstructive MHV thrombosis to determine appropriate management (repeat valve replacement or low-dose slow infusion fibrinolysis).
OAC using VKA is recommended in BHV thrombosis before considering reintervention.
